title: Positive-rate binary codes against adversarial deletions
formal:
Determine the real zero-rate threshold
\[
p^*=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:\operatorname{Ach}(p)\},
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{Ach}(p)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\exists r\in(0,1]\ \forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[n\ge N\ \land\ |C|\ge 2^{rn}\ \land\
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right].
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\) means that every codeword in \(C\) can be recovered uniquely, with zero error, after any choice of at most \(t\) deleted positions. Deleted positions are not revealed, and the adversary may know the entire code and transmitted word. The positive rate \(r\) may depend on \(p\), but must remain fixed along the unbounded sequence of block lengths. This is a question about arbitrary code families, with no efficiency, linearity or uniform construction requirement. Benchmark acceptance is absolute error at most \(1/100\) in \(p^*\).
why: This threshold is a basic information-theoretic limit for synchronization errors over the smallest nontrivial alphabet. It links the geometry of large code families to unavoidable common subsequences in binary words and separates worst-case synchronization loss from substitution and erasure models. Determining it would settle the maximum deletion fraction compatible with nonvanishing binary communication rate, independently of implementation constraints. The numerical question remains significant after the qualitative discovery that the threshold is strictly below one half.
status_note: The numerical threshold remains open in the checked primary literature. The original subsidiary question whether p*=1/2 was resolved negatively by Guruswami–He–Li (2021; inspected expanded arXiv revision 15 November 2022), but their conclusion still asks for the value of p*. An ICALP 2025 paper explicitly retains the bracket [sqrt(2)-1, 1/2-10^-40], whose width is about 0.085786 and therefore exceeds the 1/50 sufficient interval width for this benchmark. A bounded later-source search through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution or certificate meeting absolute error 1/100 for this precise model. The review inspected definitions, theorem statements and status passages, with abstract-level scope checks of newer neighboring models; it is not an exhaustive literature review, a full proof audit or a Lean verification.

importance.reason: Individual assessment: the binary adversarial deletion threshold is a central and broadly motivated coding-theoretic limit, not a tuning question for one construction. It asks when any positive-rate unique-decoding scheme can exist, connects code design to extremal subsequence structure, and survives a major qualitative upper-bound breakthrough with a substantial numerical gap. The score reflects this foundational role and scientific reach, replacing the explicitly unassessed midpoint 50.

sentences: A binary deletion code must identify every transmitted word after an adversary removes an allowed fraction of its bits without revealing their positions.
Positive rate means that codebook size grows exponentially along infinitely many block lengths with one fixed positive exponent.
The target is the supremum deletion fraction for which such zero-error uniquely decodable code families exist, with no efficiency requirement.
The checked bounds run from the square root of two minus one to one half minus ten to the minus fortieth power, and are too far apart to supply the required approximation.
An accepted answer must determine this real threshold within 1/100 and prove the accuracy in Lean, without requiring that the supremum be attained.

definitions:
A binary word of length \(n\) is a sequence \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\), with each symbol represented by one bit. A code \(C\) is a nonempty subset of these words. It may be represented by its duplicate-free lexicographically ordered list of words; no bound on the size of this representation is imposed. A message can be identified with an integer in \(\{1,\ldots,|C|\}\), encoded as the corresponding word in this list. The information rate, in bits per transmitted bit, is
\[
R(C)=\frac{\log_2|C|}{n}.
\]
Only positive block lengths \(n\ge1\) are used.

A word \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) is a subsequence of \(x\) if there are indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\) with \(y_j=x_{i_j}\) for every \(j\). The empty word is a subsequence. No surviving bit is changed or reordered. For \(0\le t\le n\), define the possible received words
\[
\mathcal D_t(x)=
\{y:\ y\text{ is a subsequence of }x,\quad n-t\le |y|\le n\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\forall x,x'\in C,\quad x\ne x'\Longrightarrow
\mathcal D_t(x)\cap\mathcal D_t(x')=\varnothing.
\]
Equivalently, a deterministic decoder from the binary words of lengths \(0,\ldots,n\) to \(C\cup\{\bot\}\) can satisfy \(D(y)=x\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(y\in\mathcal D_t(x)\), where \(\bot\) denotes failure on other inputs. The decoder may know \(C,n,t\), but receives no deletion locations. Its computation time and storage are unrestricted. Success is required for every transmitted word and every allowed deletion pattern, rather than with a small average or probabilistic error.

For two words \(x,x'\), their longest-common-subsequence length \(\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')\) is the largest integer \(m\ge0\) for which some length-\(m\) word is a subsequence of both. The correction condition is equivalent to
\[
\forall x\ne x'\in C,\qquad
\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')<n-t.
\]
For \(t=\lfloor pn\rfloor\), this is also equivalent to \(\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')<(1-p)n\), since the LCS length is an integer and \(n-\lfloor pn\rfloor=\lceil(1-p)n\rceil\). This fixes the source's suppressed rounding conventions exactly.

The predicate \(\operatorname{Ach}(p)\) uses infinitely many, equivalently arbitrarily large, block lengths. It does not require a code at every sufficiently large length. The quantified codes may be arbitrary nonlinear subsets and need not be generated by a single algorithm. The model has no shared secret, public key, feedback, random channel, stochastic encoder or list output. It is the information-theoretic unique-decoding model.

The supremum exists as a real number: the achievable set is contained in \([0,1]\) and contains \(0\), witnessed by the full binary codes. Correcting a larger deletion budget implies correcting every smaller one, so achievability is downward closed. The definition does not assert that \(p^*\) itself is achievable, or that one fixed positive rate works for fractions approaching it.
answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[
|a-p^*|\le\frac{1}{100}
\]
for the exact model and quantifiers above. The answer need not be an integer or an exactly attained deletion fraction. Merely repeating the supremum that defines \(p^*\) does not determine it.

One sufficient form is a certified interval: supply reals \(0\le l\le u\le1\), prove \(l\le p^*\le u\) and \(u-l\le1/50\), and take \(a=(l+u)/2\). The two bounds can be made fully explicit as follows:
\[
\forall p\in[0,l)\ \exists r\in(0,1]\
\forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\ge N\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[|C|\ge2^{rn}\land
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right],
\]
and
\[
\forall p\in(u,1]\ \forall r>0\
\exists N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\ge N\ \forall\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)
\Longrightarrow |C|<2^{rn}\right].
\]
All block-length variables in these statements are integers. The lower statement allows rates and families to depend on \(p\), and the upper statement ranges over every code. Neither requires attainment at an endpoint. The Lean development must establish the stated correction property and its asymptotic quantifiers, not merely verify codes at finitely many lengths.

Exact determination is welcome but is not required. A one-sided estimate, a result for efficient or linear codes alone, a different alphabet, list decoding, or probabilistic deletion errors does not by itself meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The original 2015 question asks for the value of the supremum \(p^*\), and then separately asks whether it equals \(1/2\). The present numerical target preserves that first question; it does not reinterpret the later resolution of the equality question as a determination of \(p^*\).

Bukh, Guruswami and Håstad construct positive-rate binary code families correcting every fixed deletion fraction below \(\sqrt{2}-1\). This proves \(p^*\ge\sqrt{2}-1\), without requiring that the endpoint itself be achievable.

Guruswami, He and Li prove \(p^*\le1/2-\delta_0\) for an absolute constant \(\delta_0\ge10^{-40}\). Thus the source's subsidiary question about equality with one half is resolved negatively, while the value of the threshold remains undetermined.

An ICALP 2025 primary paper explicitly retains the interval \([\sqrt{2}-1,\,1/2-10^{-40}]\) among open binary coding questions. Its width \(3/2-\sqrt{2}-10^{-40}\), approximately \(0.085786\), exceeds \(1/50\), so these checked bounds alone do not provide the benchmark's required \(1/100\) approximation.

Read the actual Guruswami–Wang APPROX/RANDOM2015 PDF: Introduction printed pp. 867–869, Section 2 p. 870 and Section 6 question1 p. 878/PDF12. The paper explicitly distinguishes random deletions, adversarial unique decoding and list decoding. Question1 first asks for p* and then separately whether it reaches one half. Positive-rate list decoding close to one half, already present in the original paper, does not answer its unique-decoding question.

Read Bukh–Guruswami–Hastad arXiv1507.01719v2, submitted 1 March 2016, title page February2016: Introduction pp. 1–2 and Theorems1–2 pp. 2–3. For every fixed epsilon>0, the construction has positive rate and corrects a fraction sqrt(2)-1-epsilon in the binary case. This establishes the lower bound on the supremum without endpoint attainment. The journal appeared in 2017; the older SODA2016 result discussed in the footnote is weaker, and the cache filename suffix2017 indicates publication rather than arXiv revision.

Read Guruswami–He–Li arXiv2106.05250v2, 15 November2022, actual definition Eq(1) printedp1/PDF2: there exists alpha_p>0 and infinitely many lengths N supporting a binary code of size at least2^(alpha_p N) with pairwise LCS<(1-p)N. This directly supports the draft's ∃r∀N0∃n≥N0 quantifiers. It would be an unjustified extra requirement to replace those with one code for every sufficiently large block length. The source has no efficiency or linearity restriction.

Read the same upper-bound source Theorem1.1 and following paragraph printedp2/PDF3. It proves p*<=1/2-delta0 for an absolute delta0>0 and explicitly records delta0>=10^-40. Section9 item1 printedp33/PDF34 still asks for the exact threshold, states the lower/upper bracket, and does not claim numerical determination. The equality-with-half subquestion is solved, but the saved numerical target is not thereby solved.

The source's LCS<(1-p)n notation is exactly compatible with at most floor(pn) deletions: the received word has length at least n-floor(pn)=ceil((1-p)n), and an integer LCS length is less than that ceiling exactly when it is less than (1-p)n. The draft defines both deletion balls and LCS so that this equivalence leaves no rounding choice to the Lean formalization.

The paper's new theorem is about Reed–Solomon/linear codes over growing alphabets, so it is a primary dated status check rather than a new binary threshold theorem. Its lower-bound attribution in that background paragraph is not used in place of reading the direct Bukh–Guruswami–Hastad source.

The real-valued Lean criterion permits abs1/100 approximation, or an interval of width1/50 with its midpoint. The lower certificate quantifies all fractions below its endpoint and arbitrarily large lengths with one rate per fraction. The upper certificate quantifies all fractions above its endpoint, every positive rate, all sufficiently large lengths and every code. These conditions accommodate a supremum not achieved by any positive-rate family. No integer-output or exact-value requirement was added.
